https://www.dw.com/en/why-is-russia-sell.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5Ht6L Russia has become one of the biggest sellers of gold as it attempts to prop up its war economy Image: Angelika Warmuth/REUTERS Advertisement Russia has sold significant volumes of its gold reserves so far in 2026 as the Kremlin seeks to raise cash to offset a big budget deficit. The Russian Central Bank announced recently that its gold reserves stood at 73.4 million troy ounces, or 2,282 metric tons, as of the start of July. That represents a decline of around 43.5 metric tonnes since the start of 2026. It means Russia's gold reserves are now at their lowest level since before the full-scale invasion of Ukraine began in February 2022. Gold prices hit record levels earlier this year , with prices averaging around $4,800 (€4,210) per ounce in the first four months before falling back to a current level of around $4,000 per ounce. Moscow's sell-off is likely to have raised more than $5 billion. "The fact that they're selling gold means that they're running out of other more liquid assets," Elina Ribakova, an economist with the Peterson Institute for International Economics, told DW. "So there is pressure on the deficit and also pressure on the sources to finance this deficit." Budget problems Russia's budget has been under serious strain in recent years due to its massively increased defense spending , which funds the war in Ukraine. Earlier this year, the Financial Times reported that the country's finance ministry had warned the cabinet in a letter that overspending on the war would be at least $28 billion in 2026, with further overspends expected in 2027 and 2028. Defense spending has more than quadrupled since 2021. It totalled around 16 trillion rubles in 2025 ($204 billion; €178 billion). Chris Weafer, a Moscow-based financial analyst with the consulting firm Macro-Advisory, says that while the Russian gold sell-off is significant, it is not a case of panic selling. "It's an extraordinary situation, but it's a relatively normal trend," he told DW. "It doesn't represent any element of Russia going broke, running out of money, not having anything else and literally selling the household silver." He says that the gold Russia has offloaded has mostly been sold by the country's finance ministry, via its National Welfare Fund (NWF), rather than the Russian Central Bank. "Since early 2022, gold was one of the assets that the National Welfare Fund could buy, because US treasuries and bunds weren't available to them (as a result of sanctions following the invasion of Ukraine)." Weafer pointed out that the asset had become a key liquid component of the fund, which, he said, was precisely what a national welfare fund is intended for: to be sold when funds are needed, particularly during difficult times. "To that extent, one can argue it is serving the intended purpose." The fund's gold sale is intended to replenish its so-called liquid assets. Weafer estimates that the fund is worth approximately $150 billion, with around $50 billion of that being described as "liquid." "The Kremlin doesn't want that buffer to go down because that would lead to maybe more speculation about financial crisis or economic difficulties, and it would undermine the Kremlin's geopolitical position," said Weafer. "It likes to portray the country as being very stable and very strong, and that $50 billion of cash is an important part of that." He says another important factor to consider is that as one of the world's biggest producers of gold, Russia can replenish stocks it has sold relatively quickly by buying from its domestic producers. Russia holds the fifth-largest reserves in the world, around the same level as China, France and Italy, and significantly behind the top two, Germany and the US. Ribakova agrees that this offers Russia a significant buffer. "Russia has an advantage," she said. "It does produce gold itself. So when it was worried about sanctions, it allocated part of the money into the gold purchases, which they were buying from the domestic producers." Funding the war for the foreseeable future The fact that Russia has become one of the biggest sellers of gold has raised further questions about its budget deficit and what that says about wider economic stability. Russia's defence budget has increased dramatically Image: Vyacheslav Prokofyev/Sputnik/AP Photo/picture alliance Russia's federal budget spending and deficit could exceed official plans by more than 1 trillion roubles ($12.85 billion) in 2026, according to ​recent government data. The budget deficit is currently projected to be 1.6% of GDP for 2026, which is approximately $40 billion, and could yet grow. However, improved revenues from oil and gas, boosted by higher oil prices due to the war in Iran, has helped Moscow to offset the budget difficulties so far in 2026. Ribakova says everything comes back to the prices and revenues Russia gets from its oil and gas, calling it the "real limit" on Moscow's capacity to finance the four-and-a-half-year-long war in Ukraine. "Everything hinges on that," she noted. "When the oil price is high, Russia gets revenues. It's easier to borrow, its domestic financial system is healthier. If the oil price drops, say, to sixty or forty, then you immediately have a crisis." Both she and Weafer caution that despite the obvious economic difficulties the Russian economy has at present, it can continue to fund the war for the foreseeable future by cutting back on non-defense spending. "Putin can continue going for years in the current environment," said Ribakova. "Maybe not making any progress on the front line, which we haven't seen any progress for the last couple of years, but still being able to throw resources at the war with Ukraine." Could Russia save the global economy? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video "Even if the deficit continues as is, Russia can still find the money and really won't be in any sort of a financial crisis or a weak geopolitical position over the next 12 to 24 months," said Weafer. Yet he points to obvious longer-term damage being done to the economy and the trouble that may bring further down the tracks. "It is creating this huge distortion in the economy and creating this longer-term negative picture that's now creating divisions in government," he said. He added that the situation had a divide between those responsible for economic growth and the Kremlin. Their message, he said, is that the current approach could not be sustained, "if you want the economy to go back to a more normal trajectory after peace. That's the bottom line." https://www.politico.eu/article/uk-labou.text: LONDON — The ruling Labour Party lost a fifth of its members last year as Keir Starmer’s government was hit by scandal, deployed unpopular policies and was forced into a raft of U-turns. The extent of the exodus from the governing party — which was led by Starmer until he resigned as prime minister in June after losing the support of his MPs — was revealed in Labour Party accounts published by the Electoral Commission Thursday. The filing shows Labour recorded a membership of 264,754 in 2025 — 20 percent lower than the 333,235 figure posted for 2024. Advertisement Advertisement Starmer faced a tricky 2025 after winning a landslide victory the previous year, which brought the center-left party back into power after 14 years. He was forced into a series of policy U-turns by his party, and sacked Peter Mandelson as U.K. ambassador to the U.S. after fresh details on the closeness of his friendship with convicted sex-trafficker Jeffrey Epstein emerged. Membership swelled under Starmer’s predecessor Jeremy Corbyn, with the party recording more than half a million Labour members at the peak of his popularity. But under Starmer and his Chancellor Rachel Reeves, the party moved rightwards economically and on issues such as immigration and benefit payments, and expelled left-leaning party stalwarts such as Corbyn and Diane Abbott. Such changes put the leadership at odds with its members, sections of whom are notably more left wing than the British public at large. The removal of the whip from several Labour MPs for voting against government welfare policies in 2024 , and again in 2025 , were watershed moments. In 2023, Starmer told members: “If you don’t like the changes that we’ve made, I say the door is open, and you can leave.” Advertisement Advertisement New Labour leader and prime minister Andy Burnham will be under pressure to reverse the decline in membership. A Labour party spokesperson said: “Labour is bringing back hope.” “The Labour Party is proud to be powered by our dedicated Party members and supporters who fight day after day for Labour victories to change the country for the better,” the spokesperson added. Labour’s declining membership comes in stark contrast to that of the left-wing Green Party, which claims its membership grew from 68,000 in September 2025 to more than 200,000 in March 2026. Many are likely to be former Labour members. It doesn’t record an official figure in its accounts. The Conservative Party does not release membership numbers, but its accounts show that its income from members dropped from £ 2.1 million in 2024 to £ 1.7 million in 2025. Joe Stanley-Smith contributed to this report. Advertisement Advertisement

Photograph: Fabrizio Bensch/Reuters Opinion Germany I know why many east Germans vote AfD. And no, it’s not an inherited longing for dictatorship Carolin Würfel Grievance politics has grown in the east of the country where I was born. But west Germans have hard questions to answer too Tue 15 Sep 2026 00.00 EDT Last modified on Tue 15 Sep 2026 04.22 EDT Share T he fear that a fascist, far-right movement would rise to power again in Germany has been with me since my youth. On 6 September, the far-right, anti-immigrant, pro-Kremlin Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) won a landslide in Saxony-Anhalt, becoming the biggest party in the state parliament, with a shocking 44% of the vote, on a record turnout. If it finds a way to power it will be the first far-right party to govern a German state since the Nazi era. The night before the vote, I sent a message to a friend, who, like myself, has an East German background. Was she as worried, scared even, about the vote as I was, I asked. I’d fallen into a loop for days, scrolling videos, reels, reports, interviews done on the ground. And I knew these AfD voters. They could have been relatives, friends of my parents, old teachers, former schoolmates. Why were they saying such incoherent stuff? I did not grow up in Saxony-Anhalt, but in Saxony – a sibling eastern German state, not entirely the same but similar in many core aspects. When I went to high school in Leipzig in the late 1990s and early 2000s, the presence of rightwing extremists was part of my coming-of-age experience. Every Friday night, you felt the fear that neo-Nazis would be waiting outside the clubs, the bars, the tram stops, fists clenched or baseball bats in hand. Every 1 May was a flashpoint when neo-Nazis were allowed to march through the city-centre. And still, Saxony’s first prime minister after reunification, Kurt Biedenkopf – a West German Christian Democratic Union (CDU) politician and a close ally of Helmut Kohl – promised, stoically, throughout his 12 years in office: “Saxony is immune to rightwing extremism.” By 2004, a year before I graduated, the far-right National Democratic party (NPD) had entered the Saxon state parliament for the first time, with 9.2% of the vote. In 2005, I left Saxony and moved to Berlin. One reason was the unbearable, dangerous presence of neo-Nazis and rightwing extremists. Many peers did the same, because it was clear that the blooming landscapes that Kohl, the German chancellor in charge of reunification, had confidently promised in 1990 weren’t going to materialise. Instead, rightwing extremism has grown steadily in eastern Germany ever since. Only the names have changed – from NPD, to Pegida (the anti-migrant protest movement launched in 2014), to AfD. I am terrified, if not surprised. Because fascist structures, left unchecked, will always keep going. But this result is also a function of the deeply troubled relationship between the former East and West Germany. A couple of weeks ago, Magnus Brechtken, deputy director of the Institut für Zeitgeschichte in Munich – Germany’s leading institute for contemporary history – gave an interview to the FAZ newspaper. It went viral. The headline: “Many west Germans have had enough now.” The interview was framed as a reminder to angry east Germans – meaning, specifically, those tempted to vote AfD out of spite towards the west – of some historical facts. Brechtken argued that the differences east Germans have been complaining about for 36 years are, by now, emotional rather than rational – the product, he suggested, of a lack of honest self-examination. He went further: the German west, he said, has spent the past 75 years proving it understands democracy and knows how to handle extremism, that it is better equipped to counter radical movements and prevent parties like the AfD from rising in the first place – while east Germans, he implied, have always had an inherited longing for authoritarian solutions. You couldn’t help but wonder how much of it was history, and how much was personal opinion. But I do think Brechtken was right about one thing. This supposed east German anger, the AfD’s popularity, the result in Saxony-Anhalt and – in all likelihood – the party’s performance in two upcoming state elections on 20 September should be used as a reminder of some actual historical facts, and of follow-up questions Brechtken apparently decided not to ask. The AfD was founded in west Germany. A large share of its leadership was born and raised in western states such as Rheinland-Pfalz and Nordrhein-Westfalen. The question shouldn’t only be what draws the east of Germany towards the AfD. It’s just as much: what draws a certain kind of west German towards building a party like this one, pushing it, and choosing the east as the place to make it grow? I believe the west German states – which officially claimed to have carried out denazification after 1945, and prided themselves on the culture of remembrance, or “coming to terms” with the Nazi past – need to look, just as urgently as the east German states, at why this fascination with fascism keeps recurring. And why, by now, are there no working structures against the rise of right-extremist movements, parties and agendas – but somehow still a system that lets them flourish? View image in fullscreen People from East and West Berlin climbing on the Wall at the Brandenburg Gate, Berlin, Germany in 1989. Photograph: imageBROKER/Alamy It’s also worth asking whether a party like the AfD went east only because east Germans are more susceptible – or because the visible inequalities there are excellent material to organise around. In 1989, a lot of east Germans had hoped for something between socialism and capitalism. Reunification wasn’t necessarily the preferred option. What followed felt, to many, badly mishandled – too fast, laws and decisions imposed rather than negotiated. And then there was the Treuhand – the agency put in charge of privatising the former GDR’s entire state-owned economy. In the process of reunification, 94% of East German companies were taken over by West German or international investors. Six per cent stayed with the people of East Germany. Six per cent. Approximately two million jobs were eliminated in the east. In the autumn and winter of 1990-91, people took to the streets again – not against their own government’s repression this time, but against the perceived occupier: West Germany. They demanded new elections, a renegotiation of the agreements that had left millions empty-handed and jobless, as unemployment in the east skyrocketed. Detlev Karsten Rohwedder, head of the Treuhand and the key figure in overhauling the former East Germany, was asked in an interview back then by a TV host: “If it doesn’t get better, aren’t you afraid there might be another revolution in East Germany?” In those years, the former East Germany was treated like a child that had to follow the laws and orders of its wiser western counterpart – a parent. Now, that child is all grown. But it remembers the experience – and quite possibly holds on to it too tightly. Ulrich Siegmund, the AfD’s man in Saxony-Anhalt, was born the same year as reunification. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to This is Europe The most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environment after newsletter promotion View image in fullscreen The AfD’s Ulrich Siegmund poses for pictures with a supporter as he campaigns in Saxony-Anhalt, 4 September 2026. Photograph: Annegret Hilse/Reuters One of his main promises is to take back control. Maybe you could say that what happened in Saxony-Anhalt went beyond a question of control and was driven by the desire for a sort of revenge. The east, finally, daring to say to the overpowering west: enough. Or as Siegmund at his first victory press conference said, the result showed that the people of Saxony-Anhalt wouldn’t be “patronised” any longer. With this he was tapping into something almost visceral. The remark also clarified for me something about the motives of the countless potential AfD voters I had listened to over the past weeks and months. Most of them don’t actually read or know what’s in the AfD’s programme. And they don’t seem to care. What won people over was simpler: I hear you. I see you. Yes, you have every right to be unhappy. Throughout the campaign, Siegmund travelled the entire state and threw parties: free sausages, free beer, dancing, music and maybe for some, it felt like the return of community. Villages and small towns that had been hollowed out, some of them ghostly and depopulated, were suddenly told again: you matter. Everyone else may have left you behind, but I, we, the AfD, care. Friedrich Merz is now on borrowed time. But that’s not why the AfD’s triumph is seismic | Jörg Lau Read more What many have not realised yet is that the AfD won’t improve life in east Germany. But that was never the point. It gave people attention in exchange for a vote. And for now, that was what counted most. Because the AfD is bigger than east versus west. It was built by west Germans, carried by east Germans, and now it strives for power across the country. Its programme runs on ideas Germany once needed a war and total defeat to bury: racism, the belief in superiority and a hierarchy of who really belongs, contempt for who doesn’t, a hunger for enemies dressed up as pride. That’s not a regional problem. It’s a national one, and it should frighten every single German citizen. A vote for the AfD is a vote for that same set of beliefs. Whatever anger, disappointment, or legitimate demand to finally be seen or heard got bundled in alongside it. In April 1932, the Nazi party became the strongest party in the state election in the region that now makes up Saxony-Anhalt, with 40.7% of the vote, and formed, with coalition partners, the first Nazi-led state government in Germany. Whatever happens next, it will be hard to say we didn’t know. Carolin Würfel is a writer, screenwriter and journalist Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article?
